evidence: reserve() checks `line.quantity > product.availableQuantity` for all lines before reserving any of them, which is an all-or-nothing stock rule and a domain responsibility.
State changes are handed to the aggregate through `product.reserve(line.quantity)` and `product.release(line.quantity)`.
The only data access is through `ProductRepository` (findById, save), imported from ./product-repository inside the domain layer. The file has no SQL, ORM, transport or framework code.
Errors are raised as `DomainError` with domain codes ('INSUFFICIENT_STOCK', 'NOT_FOUND'), not as HTTP or transport errors.
In the graph, the application use cases (PlaceOrderUseCase, CancelOrderUseCase) inject this service, which fits a domain service that application code orchestrates.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: This file passes. StockAllocationService is a domain service, and its work is domain work: it enforces the stock-availability rule across several order lines, checking every line before changing any product. It hands the actual reserve and release changes to the Product aggregate, and it reports rule violations as DomainError. It reaches stored data only through ProductRepository, an abstraction declared in the domain layer itself. The file contains no database, ORM, HTTP or framework code. Calling `this.products.save(product)` from a domain service is debatable, since some would leave saving to the application layer. But it goes through a domain-owned port and adds no persistence mechanics, so it is not misplaced infrastructure logic. No ADR text was provided that forbids domain services from using repositories.
